## Section 1. Spin bundles, correspondence space, and local flattening of \((F,D_\alpha)\)

### 1.1. Conformal spin geometry in four complex dimensions

Let \((M,[g])\) be a complex four–manifold equipped with a holomorphic conformal structure. We assume \(M\) is (locally) spin so that the conformal frame bundle lifts and the complexified tangent bundle admits a spinor factorization
\[
TM \;\cong\; V_+ \otimes V_-,
\]
where \(V_+\to M\) and \(V_-\to M\) are rank–\(2\) holomorphic vector bundles (“unprimed” and “primed” spin bundles). We use abstract spinor indices \(A,B,\dots\) for \(V_+\) and \(A',B',\dots\) for \(V_-\). A choice of representative metric \(g\in[g]\) is equivalent to choosing symplectic forms \(\varepsilon_{AB}\) on \(V_+\) and \(\varepsilon_{A'B'}\) on \(V_-\), inducing
\[
g_{AA'BB'}=\varepsilon_{AB}\,\varepsilon_{A'B'}.
\]
Fixing \(g\) also determines the Levi–Civita connection \(\nabla\), hence induced connections on \(V_\pm\). (Everything below can be phrased conformally using the normal conformal Cartan connection; for Section 1 it is enough to work in a local scale \(g\) and note which statements are conformally invariant.) fileciteturn0file13turn0file10

### 1.2. The correspondence space \(F=\mathbb P(V_-)\)

Define the correspondence space
\[
F \;:=\; \mathbb P(V_-)\,,
\]
the bundle of complex projective lines in \(V_-\). Write \(\pi:F\to M\) for the projection. A point of \(F\) is \((x,[\pi_{A'}])\) where \(x\in M\) and \([\pi_{A'}]\in \mathbb P(V_{-,x})\cong\mathbb{CP}^1\).

Let \(\pi_{A'}\) be a local homogeneous representative of \([\pi_{A'}]\). Over \(F\) there is the tautological line subbundle \(\mathcal O_{F}(-1)\subset \pi^*V_-\), spanned by \(\pi_{A'}\). Using \(\nabla\), we can differentiate \(\pi_{A'}\) along directions tangent to \(F\); in particular, along vectors that project to \(TM\).

### 1.3. The \(\alpha\)-plane distribution \(D_\alpha\)

On \(F\), define a rank–\(2\) distribution \(D_\alpha\subset TF\) as follows. For each unprimed spinor \(\lambda^A\), consider the corresponding null vector in \(TM\):
\[
v^{AA'} = \lambda^A \pi^{A'} \in (V_+\otimes V_-)_{x}.
\]
There is a canonical way to lift \(v\) to a vector on \(F\): take the **horizontal lift** with respect to the connection on \(V_-\) induced by \(\nabla\), and require that the lift preserve the line \([\pi]\) (equivalently, preserve the tautological subbundle). Concretely, \(D_\alpha\) is locally spanned by vector fields
\[
L_A \;:=\; \pi^{A'} \nabla_{AA'} \quad (A=0,1),
\]
viewed as vector fields on \(F\) (i.e. acting on functions on \(F\), where \(\nabla\) includes the induced action on the fiber coordinate \([\pi]\)). This is the standard curved correspondence-space version of the flat Lax pair. fileciteturn0file10turn0file13

Interpretation: at \((x,[\pi])\in F\), the image \(\pi_*(D_\alpha)\subset T_xM\) is the 2-plane
\[
\Pi_\alpha(x,[\pi]) := \{\lambda^A\pi^{A'}:\lambda^A\in V_{+,x}\},
\]
a totally null \(\alpha\)-plane in the tangent space (in the conformal sense). Hence \(D_\alpha\) is the “tautological \(\alpha\)-plane distribution” on \(\mathbb P(V_-)\).

### 1.4. Frobenius integrability and anti-self-duality

The key structural fact is that the Frobenius condition for \(D_\alpha\) is equivalent to the (anti-)self-duality of the Weyl curvature.

**Proposition 1.1 (Integrability criterion).**  
\(D_\alpha\) is involutive (i.e. \([D_\alpha,D_\alpha]\subset D_\alpha\)) if and only if the primed Weyl spinor vanishes:
\[
\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0,
\]
i.e. the conformal structure is **anti-self-dual** in the standard spinor convention.

*Sketch.* One computes \([L_A,L_B]\) using the commutator of covariant derivatives and projects onto the vertical directions of \(\mathbb P(V_-)\). The vertical component is governed precisely by the curvature of the induced connection on \(V_-\), whose trace-free part is \(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}\). Thus the obstruction to involutivity is the primed Weyl curvature. This is the usual “\(\alpha\)-surface Frobenius theorem” in curved twistor theory. fileciteturn0file10turn0file13turn0file9

When \(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0\), the integral manifolds of \(D_\alpha\) project to \(\alpha\)-surfaces in \(M\), and the leaf space (when well-behaved) becomes the twistor space. Locally, this is the starting point of the nonlinear graviton correspondence. fileciteturn0file9turn0file10

### 1.5. Local existence of generalized self-dual (isothermal) coordinates

We now state the local existence result in the form you want for Section 1: **a local identification of the filtered manifold \((F,D_\alpha)\) with the flat correspondence space**.

Let \((\mathbf M,\mathbf F,\mathbf D_\alpha)\) denote the flat model, where \(\mathbf M=\mathbb C^4\) and \(\mathbf F=\mathbf M\times \mathbb{CP}^1\) with the standard distribution
\[
\mathbf L_A = \pi^{A'} \frac{\partial}{\partial x^{AA'}} \quad (A=0,1),
\qquad
\mathbf D_\alpha = \mathrm{span}\{\mathbf L_0,\mathbf L_1\}.
\]

**Theorem 1.2 (Local flattening of the correspondence space).**  
Let \((M,[g])\) be a complex conformal 4–manifold with \(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0\) on an open set \(U\subset M\). Then for every \(p\in U\) there exist neighborhoods
\[
p\in U_0\subset U,\qquad (p,[\pi_0])\in \mathcal U\subset F|_{U_0},
\]
and a biholomorphism
\[
\Phi:\mathcal U \longrightarrow \mathcal U_{\mathrm{flat}}\subset \mathbf F
\]
such that
\[
\Phi_*(D_\alpha)=\mathbf D_\alpha.
\]
Equivalently, \((F,D_\alpha)\) is locally isomorphic, as a rank–2 Frobenius system, to the flat correspondence space.

*Proof (coordinate construction).* Because \(D_\alpha\) is involutive, through each \((p,[\pi_0])\) there passes a 2-dimensional leaf \(\Sigma\subset F\) tangent to \(D_\alpha\). Choose local coordinates \((u^0,u^1)\) on \(\Sigma\) so that \(L_A=\partial/\partial u^A\) along \(\Sigma\). Extend \((u^0,u^1)\) to a coordinate system on \(\mathcal U\) by adding two transverse coordinates \((v^0,v^1)\) and a fiber coordinate \([\pi]\) on \(\mathbb{CP}^1\). In these adapted coordinates, \(D_\alpha\) is spanned by vector fields of the form
\[
L_A=\frac{\partial}{\partial u^A}+\sum_{i=0}^1 a_{A}^{\,i}(u,v,[\pi])\frac{\partial}{\partial v^i}
+\;b_A(u,v,[\pi])\,\frac{\partial}{\partial [\pi]}.
\]
Now use the freedom of changing \((v^0,v^1)\) by solving transport equations along the leaves to kill the \(\partial/\partial v^i\) components, and use the projective freedom in \([\pi]\) together with the induced connection on \(V_-\) to normalize \(b_A\) to the flat value. The resulting coordinates yield a map \(\Phi\) to \(\mathbf F\) that sends the span of \(\{L_A\}\) to the span of \(\{\mathbf L_A\}\).

This is a standard “straightening” argument for Frobenius systems, but the content here is that the system is **canonically defined from the conformal spin connection** and becomes Frobenius exactly under ASD curvature; hence the straightening produces what you are calling generalized self-dual/isothermal coordinates on the correspondence space. (The corresponding statement downstairs on \(M\) is recovered by projecting \(\Phi\) along \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) and interpreting the induced incidence relations.) fileciteturn0file10turn0file13turn0file15

### 1.6. Remarks for the rest of the paper

1. **What is being “flattened.”** The theorem is best read as: the curved data \((M,[g])\) with \(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0\) gives a canonical rank–2 integrable distribution \(D_\alpha\) on \(F=\mathbb P(V_-)\), and *that* Frobenius system is locally equivalent to the flat one. This is the precise replacement for “flat isothermal coordinates” in this setting. fileciteturn0file15

2. **Connection language.** If you want the Cartan emphasis: \(D_\alpha\) is the distribution annihilated by the “incidence” 1-forms \(\pi^{A'}\theta_{AA'}\) (with \(\theta\) the solder form) together with the requirement of horizontality for the induced \(V_-\)-connection; involutivity is the vanishing of the relevant curvature component. This aligns well with a later move to conformal Cartan geometry.

3. **Bridge to twistor space.** Once \((F,D_\alpha)\) is straightened, taking the local leaf space gives a local complex 3–fold \(PT\) and recovers the nonlinear graviton picture. This is where you can connect the “coordinate charts identifying \((F,D_\alpha)\) with the flat correspondence space” to “coordinate patches of twistor space mapping into \(\mathbb C^3\)” as in your draft narrative. fileciteturn0file9turn0file10turn0file15

If you want, the next natural step is to decide whether Section 1 ends **at Theorem 1.2** (pure correspondence-space flattening), or whether you also want an explicit **downstairs formulation**: a local coordinate system on \(M\) (plus a gauge choice on \(V_-\)) in which the operators \(L_A=\pi^{A'}\nabla_{AA'}\) take a canonical “flat + lower-order” form. That’s often the cleanest bridge into “generalized coordinates on \(M\)” in Section 2.

Yes this is a good start, but actually I think the main content of the section is the form of the system on the flat space. In particular I expect that all of the curvature will be embodied in a single chiral spin connection acting on the left (perhaps satisfying an additional condition). It will be necessary to recover this on the flat space. This actually could create some subtlety in the argument you gave, because as far as I can tell you constructed the coordinates locally on the correspondence space, but to define a connection on the flat space I think the map might necessarily be defined globally on each fiber of the flat correspondence space. This is normally how it works for reconstructing connections, for example in the Penrose Ward construction.  This may require some assumptions about the domains of the maps, namely that they are globally defined on each fiber in the flat space in some neighborhood. Let me know what you think about this.

You are exactly right to flag this. There are really **two different “flattening” problems** that people sometimes conflate:

1. **Frobenius straightening of a rank–2 distribution** \(D_\alpha\) on a 5-fold \(F\). This is inherently *local on \(F\)* and only needs a small neighborhood of a single point \((x,[\pi])\).

2. **Reconstruction of a (chiral) connection on the base** from a family of \(\alpha\)-planes parametrized by a *whole* \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) over each \(x\). This is the Ward/nonlinear-graviton logic: the compactness of the line and global holomorphicity along it is what lets you identify the curvature as a cohomology/patching datum (or as a splitting problem). That demands a neighborhood in \(F\) that contains **entire fibers** \(\mathbb{P}(V_{-,x})\) for \(x\) in some neighborhood.

So yes: the “local on \(F\)” straightening argument I sketched is insufficient for what you want if the section’s main content is “all curvature sits in a single chiral spin connection acting on the left, recovered on the flat side.”

### What I think the correct fix is

You should explicitly distinguish:

- a **pointwise** local equivalence \((F,D_\alpha)\sim(\mathbf F,\mathbf D_\alpha)\) near \((x,[\pi_0])\); versus  
- a **fiberwise** local equivalence over a neighborhood \(U\subset M\):
  \[
  \Phi:\ \pi^{-1}(U)=\mathbb P(V_-)|_U \longrightarrow U_{\mathrm{flat}}\times\mathbb{CP}^1
  \]
  defined on *all* \([\pi]\in\mathbb{CP}^1\) for each \(x\in U\), with \(\Phi_*(D_\alpha)=\mathbf D_\alpha\).

Only the second one is strong enough to support “recover the left chiral connection on flat space” in the Penrose–Ward sense.

### Why the fiberwise condition is nontrivial

Even if \(D_\alpha\) is integrable, the coefficients of the Lax pair
\[
L_A=\pi^{A'}\nabla_{AA'}
\]
are, a priori, only defined as **holomorphic vector fields on \(F\)**. When you push them forward to the *flat* correspondence space, you typically want a form like
\[
\Phi_* L_A \;=\; \pi^{A'}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{AA'}} + \Gamma_{AA'}{}^{B}{}_{C}(x)\,(\cdot)\Big)
\]
where the only nontrivial data is a **left (unprimed) connection** \(\Gamma_{AA'}{}^{B}{}_{C}\) (chiral spin connection), and crucially that \(\Gamma\) is independent of \([\pi]\). To justify “independent of \([\pi]\)” you need control of the \([\pi]\)-dependence globally on \(\mathbb{CP}^1\).

This is exactly the same place where Ward’s construction needs “trivial on every line” and where splitting arguments use \(H^1(\mathbb{CP}^1,\mathcal O(k))\).

### A clean way to state the needed hypothesis (and it matches your intuition)

What you likely want is an explicit **regularity-in-\([\pi]\)** assumption that turns a priori local data into something global along each fiber.

A good formulation is:

> **(Fiber-regularity)** On \(\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb{CP}^1\) (after choosing a local spin frame for \(V_-\)), the vector fields spanning \(D_\alpha\) can be written as
> \[
> L_A=\pi^{A'}\Big(e_{AA'}^{\ \ \mu}(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}\Big)\;+\;(\text{vertical part}),
> \]
> where the coefficients are **holomorphic functions of \([\pi]\)** on all of \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) (i.e. no poles in any affine chart).

Because \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) is compact, “holomorphic on all of \(\mathbb{CP}^1\)” forces the allowed dependence to be a **global section** of some \(\mathcal O(k)\). In practice (with the usual homogeneities) that collapses the freedom drastically, and is exactly what makes the “everything lives in a single chiral connection” statement possible.

In other words: the subtlety you pointed out becomes a *feature*: it tells you the theorem you want is not just “Frobenius ⇒ local straightening,” but “Frobenius + fiber-regularity ⇒ fiberwise flattening and chiral connection extraction.”

### What the section can then prove (suggested Theorem package)

I would structure Section 1 around two theorems:

**Theorem A (Frobenius / ASD).**  
\(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0 \iff D_\alpha\) is integrable.

**Theorem B (Fiberwise flattening and chiral remainder).**  
Assume \(\Psi_{A'B'C'D'}=0\) on \(U\) and the fiber-regularity condition above. Then there exists a fiber-preserving biholomorphism
\[
\Phi:\ \mathbb P(V_-)|_U \to U_{\mathrm{flat}}\times\mathbb{CP}^1
\]
such that in the induced trivialization on the flat side the operators take the form
\[
\Phi_*L_A=\pi^{A'}\Big(\partial_{AA'} + \Gamma_{AA'}(x)\Big),
\]
where \(\Gamma_{AA'}(x)\) is a connection acting only on unprimed indices (the “left” chiral spin connection), and it satisfies the expected self-duality condition (the remaining curvature lives in the left sector).

This makes the **main content** of the section exactly what you said: “the flat system, with curvature encoded in a single chiral connection.”

### Practical comment: how to ensure the fiberwise domain exists

Locally on \(M\), \(\mathbb P(V_-)\) is always *topologically* a product \(U\times\mathbb{CP}^1\) after choosing a local frame of \(V_-\). The real analytic/holo issue is: do your coordinates / flattening map develop poles in \([\pi]\)?

So it’s perfectly reasonable (and, honestly, standard) to build into the definition of “generalized isothermal coordinates” something like:

- the map is defined on \(\pi^{-1}(U)\) (full fibers),
- it is holomorphic in \([\pi]\) globally on \(\mathbb{CP}^1\),
- and has the correct homogeneity.

That is precisely the analogue of “bundle trivial on each twistor line” in Ward.

---

If you want, I can rewrite Section 1 accordingly: make the *flat system* the protagonist, introduce the two-tier notion (“pointwise flattening” vs “fiberwise flattening”), and then state Theorem B with a crisp “fiber-regularity / no poles on \(\mathbb{CP}^1\)” hypothesis that later becomes your **key condition** for extracting the chiral connection. That will also set you up to mirror Ward’s reconstruction arguments without actually needing the full global twistor space.
